message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Report problems in writing (email or certified mail).
• If the landlord fails to fix, you may:
 • Withhold rent (after giving notice),
 • Pay for repairs and deduct from rent,
 • File a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local code enforcement. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (no more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Keep receipts or bank records.
• If you’re late, notify the landlord in writing and ask for a grace period if possible. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: The landlord can’t terminate early unless you breach the lease or the landlord has a valid legal reason (e.g., non‑payment, illegal activity). | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail).
• Keep a copy of the notice. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice of entry.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint or seek a court order. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • Report discrimination to the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may pay for the repair and deduct the cost from your rent (but only after giving notice and a reasonable time to fix). | • Keep receipts and provide a written notice to the landlord before paying. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must follow the Texas **eviction procedure**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• The landlord cannot evict you without a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly.
• If you receive an eviction notice, you can file a **motion to dismiss** or **motion for summary judgment** in the county court. | | **Rent Control & Rent Increases** | • Texas has **no statewide rent control**. Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the systems. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Insurance** | • Tenants are not required by law to carry renters’ insurance, but it’s highly recommended. | • Obtain a policy covering personal property and liability. | | **Legal Assistance** | • **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** offers resources and can mediate disputes.
• **Legal Aid of North Texas**, **Texas Legal Services**, and local bar associations provide free or low‑cost legal help. | • Contact TDHCA or a local legal aid office for guidance. | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease** – Understand rent amount, due date, security deposit limits, pet policies, and notice requirements. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and inspection reports. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – 30 days for month‑to‑month termination, 24–48 hours for entry, 3 days for non‑payment eviction notice. 4. **Report Issues Promptly** – Write a formal notice to the landlord; keep a copy. 5. **Seek Mediation if Needed** – Use TDHCA or local mediation services before filing a lawsuit. 6. **Know Your Rights to Discrimination** – Report any discriminatory actions to TCHR or HUD. --- #### When to Call a Lawyer - You receive an eviction notice and want to contest it. - The landlord refuses to make necessary repairs. - You suspect unlawful rent increases or deposit deductions. - You experience discrimination or harassment. A lawyer can help you file the correct motions, negotiate settlements, or represent you in court. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general and not legal advice. Laws can change, and specific circumstances may alter your rights. For personalized guidance, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant advocacy organization.
